summary.text: A healthy 28-year-old primigravida delivered a male infant at 40 gestational weeks after an uncomplicated delivery with mediolateral episiotomy. She then entered shock with hypotension from atonic bleeding, with residual placenta found on examination and sonography. Emergency curettage under general anesthesia removed it.

Atony was treated with oxytocin, sulprostone, misoprostol, a Bakri balloon for 24 h, tranexamic acid, fibrinogen and two erythrocyte concentrates; total blood loss was 2500 ml and bleeding stopped. After overnight monitoring she moved to the ward. On the first postpartal day she had hot flashes, headache and agalactorrhea, then polydipsia and polyuria on the second.

Laboratory tests showed hypernatremia, hyperchloremia, serum hyperosmolality and low urinary osmolality, leading to a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. Brain MRI on the third day showed mild pituitary infarction compatible with Sheehan syndrome; hormone assessment showed partial hypopituitarism with hypothyroidism and Addison’s disease, low gonadotropins and high prolactin. Hemoglobin fell to 6.5 g/dl and three erythrocyte concentrates were given.

Desmopressin nasal spray from the fourth day normalized urine production, with transient hyponatremia during daily use that resolved after a 3-day pause. She also received l-thyroxine, hydrocortisone and sequential estradiol and progesterone replacement, and was discharged in stable condition 13 days after delivery. At six weeks hormone levels were reported normalized; at four months she felt well with partial diabetes insipidus on desmopressin.
